rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the evidence and points straight at the missing proof: "the most newsworthy fact is what is NOT yet known (the post-relaunch paying-user trend)." B has usable instincts, but it decorates too freely, especially "Bumble is the highest-profile dating platform to deploy AI matchmaking and AI-assisted message writing at scale." That is how a real angle turns into a fact-check problem with nice shoes.
gaps_in_A: "Dating apps add AI to write your opening line" over-broadens a one-company fact into a category claim. A adds a caution later, but the headline still gets ahead of the evidence.

"hands message-writing to AI" is sharper than the supplied mechanics. The update says the feature helps users write openings, not that AI authors them or that it touches women's first messages specifically.
"Dorsey/Schultz/Kalanick-adjacent" is insider shorthand and one comparison is messy. The founder-return angle does not need name-dropping to work.
gaps_in_B: "Bumble is the highest-profile dating platform to deploy AI matchmaking and AI-assisted message writing at scale" is invented. No competitor landscape, scale, or profile ranking was supplied.
"Is Bumble's Women-First Model Still Feminist?" imports "feminist" and agency/control framing that is not in the update, then overclaims that the tension "is built into the product, not speculative."
"The relaunch is the stated answer to the subscriber slide" overstates company intent. The facts only say the relaunch follows declining paying users and a falling stock price.
"user backlash is already on record" turns "some users have criticized AI in dating" into a stronger, Bumble-specific record than the facts support.
